name: Alumkadavu boat‑building yards (kettuvallam)
tagline: Watch traditional kettuvallam (houseboat) construction on Ashtamudi Lake
summary: Alumkadavu is a backwater village on Ashtamudi Lake where traditional kettuvallam and wooden boats are still handcrafted; visitors can watch open‑sided yards and learn the ties-to-coir craft behind…
description: Alumkadavu is a quiet boatyard village on the Ashtamudi backwaters in Karunagappally (Kollam). The open‑sided yards on the bank still build and refit kettuvallams — the long, coir‑sewn wooden barges that became Kerala’s houseboats.

The village matters because it preserved the craft knowledge that allowed the modern Kerala houseboat to be created: the 1991 conversion that launched Kerala’s houseboat industry was done with the help of an Alumkadavu carpenter. Today the yards still use traditional joinery, coir caulking and local timbers.

For a visitor the yards offer a close, working view of boatbuilding: hull ribs, planks being shaped, coir ropes and packing, thatched roofs, and the human scale of a craft that moved rice and coir before roads took over. Yards are private worksites — people watch, photograph and learn, but should be courteous and keep to the edge of the site.
highlights: Open‑sided boatyards where you can watch kettuvallam hulls and roofs take shape
See traditional techniques: planks joined and tied with coir, coir caulking and thatch roofing
Direct link to the 1991 Kerala houseboat conversion (local carpenter worked with tour operators)
Part of the Ashtamudi backwater circuit — easy to combine with a Kollam–Alappuzha boat run
Village coir industry and riverside craft atmosphere

sections.heading: Background
body: Alumkadavu is a small backwater settlement near Karunagappally (Kollam) known for traditional wooden boat and kettuvallam building. The kettuvallam was originally a cargo barge; when road freight declined the craft nearly died but survived in yards like Alumkadavu.

The specific conversion that created the modern Kerala cruising houseboat dates to 1991, when a tour operator worked with an Alumkadavu carpenter to refit a freight kettuvallam into a moving guest vessel — the design then spread across Kerala’s backwaters.

sections.heading: The craft — how kettuvallams are made
body: Kettuvallam construction is a handcraft of wood, coir and thatch. Planks (local timbers such as anjili/jack are used historically) are edge‑joined and drawn together with coir lashings; seams are caulked with coir fibre. Roofs are traditionally arched and thatched; interiors are fitted for guests when boats are converted to houseboats.

Although the brochure line 'no nails, only coir ties' describes the traditional method, many modern vessels mix old techniques with newer materials in places — but the visible process at the yards (ribs, lashings, coir work) is still a living craft.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Walk the public bank to view half‑finished hulls propped on blocks, craftsmen shaping planks, coir being packed into seams and thatch being woven for roofs. Yards are working sites, so watch from a respectful distance, ask before photographing or stepping inside, and expect informal explanations from builders if they are free.

Combine a visit with a backwater cruise or the DTPC Kollam public boat between Kollam and Alappuzha (Alumkadavu is a common stop). Several small resorts and homestays on the bank can arrange a guided yard visit or a short boat trip to see the yards from the water.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Nearest town and rail access: Karunagappally (railway station about 3–6 km away). Buses run from Kollam and Karunagappally to the Alumkadavu area. The nearest major airports are Trivandrum or Kochi; allow road time from either.

There are no formal visitor facilities at the yards — they are private workshops. Ask before you enter or photograph; wear shoes suitable for uneven, muddy ground; keep clear of moving timber and tools. If you want a guided explanation, ask a local resort, homestay or the District Tourism Promotion Council (DTPC) Kollam to arrange a short yard visit.

latest.text: Updated Roampedia guide corrects common origin myths about 'first houseboat in India', explains Alumkadavu’s role in the 1991 Kerala houseboat conversion and advises visitors to ask permission before entering yards.

visitorInfo.howToReach: Go via Karunagappally (nearest rail/road hub); buses and short taxis connect to Alumkadavu. DTPC/Kollam boat runs the Kollam–Alappuzha route and commonly stops at Alumkadavu for a break.
etiquette: Yards are working sites — ask before you step in or photograph and keep a safe distance from tools and timber.
Wear closed shoes and bring a light raincoat if travel is during shoulder/monsoon months — banks can be muddy.
If you want explanation or a guided look, ask your hotel/homestay or DTPC Kollam to arrange a short visit.
Respect local workers’ space and bargaining: this is their livelihood, not a staged attraction.
